questions.title: Why does the entropy patching function need both a global threshold \(\theta_g\) and an approximate monotonic constraint \(\theta_r\)?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.3 the paper describes two ways to locate patch boundaries using next‑byte entropies \(H(x_i)\): one based on a global entropy threshold \(H(x_t) > \theta_g\) and another based on the increase relative to the previous byte \(H(x_t) - H(x_{t-1}) > \theta_r\). I understand that both aim to identify high‑uncertainty positions, but I am unclear on the intuition behind using both criteria together. How does the monotonic constraint complement the global threshold? In practice, does one dominate the other or are they combined in a specific way during preprocessing?

questions.title: How is the “incremental patching” property formally defined and why does BPE fail to satisfy it?
questions.question_body: The paper defines incremental patching as \(f_p(\mathbf{x}_{<i}) = f_p(\mathbf{x})_{<i}\). Could someone explain in plain terms what this equation means for a streaming generation scenario? Additionally, why does a standard BPE tokenizer not meet this property? I see a footnote mentioning a delimiter token could turn BPE into an incremental scheme, but I am not sure how that would work without increasing sequence length.

questions.title: What exactly is the role of the cross‑attention layer in the Local Encoder and how are queries initialized?
questions.question_body:
In Section 4.2 it is stated that each transformer layer in the encoder is followed by a cross‑attention module that pools byte representations into patch representations. The query vector for a patch is said to be "initialized by pooling the byte representations corresponding to that patch". Could anyone clarify:
1. What pooling operation is used (e.g., max‑pooling, mean‑pooling)?
2. How does this query initialization interact with subsequent cross‑attention steps?
3. Why is this cross‑attention needed given that patches already contain grouped bytes?

questions.title: Why are hash n‑gram embeddings used instead of learned n‑gram embeddings in the encoder?
questions.question_body: Section 4.2.1 introduces hash embeddings for byte n‑grams of size 3–8 using a RollPolyHash function. The authors mention frequency‑based n‑gram embeddings as an alternative explored in an appendix. What are the advantages of hash embeddings (e.g., memory efficiency, collision handling) over directly learning an embedding table for all possible n‑grams? Also, how sensitive is model performance to the hash table size (e.g., 100K vs 500K entries) according to their ablations?

questions.title: How does average patch size affect both training context length and inference FLOPs?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that larger average patch sizes reduce inference FLOPs because the Latent Transformer runs fewer steps, yet they also keep "the number of bytes in each batch constant in expectation" when changing patch size. I'm confused about how increasing patch size simultaneously reduces compute per token while preserving context length. Does changing the average patch size implicitly shorten the sequence length fed to the Global Transformer? How is this accounted for in their FLOP estimation formula (Equation 5)?

questions.title: Can someone walk through the FLOP per byte equation for BLT and explain each term?
questions.question_body:
In Section 4.5 the authors provide a multi‑line expression for \(\text{FL}_{\text{BLT}}\) involving functions \(\text{Transf. FL}(\cdot)\) and \(\text{Cross Attn. FL}(\cdot)\). I am not familiar with their notation:
- What do parameters \(h_{\mathcal{G}}, l_{\mathcal{G}}, n_{ctx}, n_p\) represent?
- How is \(m=n_{ctx}/n_p\) derived?
- Why is there a factor \(k/n_p\) multiplied after Cross‑Attention FLOPs?
A step‑by‑step breakdown would help me understand how they compute FLOPs per byte.

questions.title: Why do the authors treat embedding lookups as zero‑FLOP operations?
questions.question_body: In Section 4.5 they state "we assume the input embedding layer is implemented as an efficient lookup instead of a dense matrix multiplication, therefore becoming a 0‑flop operation." Is this assumption realistic for modern hardware where embedding lookups still incur memory bandwidth costs? How might this simplification affect comparisons between BLT and token‑based models where embeddings have different dimensions?

questions.title: How does Bits‑Per‑Byte (BPB) relate to traditional perplexity for byte‑level models?
questions.question_body: The paper reports BPB as \(\text{BPB}(x)= \frac{\mathcal{L}_{CE}(\mathbf{x})}{\ln(2) \cdot n_{\text{bytes}}}\). I know perplexity is exp(loss per token), but I'm unsure how BPB translates to an intuitive measure of model quality. For example, what BPB value corresponds roughly to a perplexity of 20 on a tokenizer with average token length 4 bytes? Also, can BPB be compared across datasets with different byte distributions?

questions.title: What is meant by “block‑causal” attention in the Global Transformer and how does it differ from standard causal attention?
questions.question_body: Section 4 mentions that the Latent Global Transformer uses a block‑causal mask (citing Dubey et al., 2024). How exactly does block‑causal mask work when patches have variable lengths? Does it restrict attention only within each block/patch or across patches up to current one? A concrete example illustrating attention patterns would be helpful.

questions.title: Why does resetting the entropy model context with new lines improve entropy drift during training?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.3 they note that "entropy drift" occurs when using long contexts with entropy patching, so they reset entropy context at new lines for large‑scale runs. How does resetting mitigate drift mathematically? Does it simply bound the window over which next‑byte entropy is computed or also affect model bias toward certain structures?

questions.title: What are the trade‑offs between static strided patching (fixed K) and dynamic entropy patching regarding model capacity allocation?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that static strided patching wastes compute on easy regions (e.g., whitespace) while dynamic entropy patching allocates more compute where entropy is high. However, could dynamic patching lead to excessively short patches on noisy data, thereby increasing Global Transformer steps? How do they ensure that average patch size remains controlled while still adapting to local complexity?

questions.title: How does BLT handle generation when encountering a new unseen byte sequence that could belong to multiple possible patches?
questions.question_body: During inference, BLT must decide whether it is at a patch boundary before invoking the latent transformer. If a novel byte sequence appears that has ambiguous entropy (e.g., due to noise), what mechanism determines whether to start a new patch or continue aggregating bytes? Is there any fallback or confidence threshold used at generation time?

questions.title: Why does increasing both model size and average patch size simultaneously improve scaling under a fixed inference FLOP budget?
questions.question_body: Section 6 states that using larger patches saves compute which can be reallocated to grow the Global Transformer while keeping inference FLOPs constant. Intuitively I would think larger patches reduce granularity and possibly degrade performance on fine‑grained predictions. How do empirical results reconcile this trade‑off? Is there evidence that larger patches only affect easy parts of data while harder parts still get enough steps?

questions.#title: What modifications are required to convert an existing tokenizer‑based LLM into a BLT model via "byte‑ifying" as described in Section 7?
questions.#question_body: The authors mention initializing BLT’s global transformer with weights from Llama 3 1T and then training with lower learning rates for those parameters while training local modules more aggressively. Are there any architectural mismatches (e.g., embedding dimensions or vocabularies) that need adaptation? How are token embeddings replaced by byte embeddings during this process?

questions.#title: How does FlexAttention enable efficient implementation of dynamic cross‑attention masks in BLT?
questions.#question_body: The paper says FlexAttention provides fused implementations for cross‑attention layers involving dynamic masks based on variable‐size patches. Could someone explain what FlexAttention does under the hood compared to standard FlashAttention? Does it precompute mask patterns or use sparse kernels, and how critical is it for training speed?

questions.#title: In the ablation study for n‑gram hash embeddings (Table X), why do diminishing returns appear after ~300K hashes at 8B scale?
questions.#question_body: The authors report that increasing hash table size from 100K to 500K leads to noticeable BPB improvements up to ~300K entries but then plateaus at 0.001 BPB gain for larger tables. Is this due primarily to hash collisions becoming rare after a certain capacity, or are there other factors such as limited receptive field of local encoder limiting usefulness of additional n‑gram contexts?
